problem_statement.text: Retrieval fails when people remember a simple cue (often a single noun or named entity) but Google Photos’ search does not interpret or match it, showing irrelevant/over-broad or zero results or burying the right photo.

chain.text: Within the 115 core stories, 31 of 115 (27%) first fail at search matching [stage5], a large block that, if mitigated, could raise the share of coded public stories that reach “nothing went wrong” [stage9] (38 of 115).

Evidence patterns point to underspecified queries and mismatch: first queries are often single nouns (19) versus several keywords (4); what users saw was frequently irrelevant (6), far too many (3), or zero results (2); quotes describe off-target hits and having to scroll to finally find the photo.
Candidate [stage5] — “Search did not understand or match what they typed” — passes both gates, ranks first on headline score, and remains rank-1 across 100% of weight-sensitivity draws.

Root cause signaled in public stories: search misparses entities, lacks or misses concepts/objects, applies logic that shrinks recall, or buries matches below the fold; combined with terse queries, the right photo is not surfaced where it can be recognized.

why_not_top.text: Although 20 of 115 core stories first fail at library state [stage0] and adjacent talk is dominated by photos that were gone (130 of 216), this candidate is gated out as not addressable by search/AI for retrieval (deleted or never uploaded), and it is smaller than [stage5] in core stories (31 vs 20).

target_segment.direction: Focus first on sentimental and “unclear-why-kept” memories; do not commit yet to utility-only cases.

why.text: Among [stage5] core stories, photo types are sentimental 13, unclear 15, utility 3; in the core base overall, sentimental 48 (42%), unclear 46 (40%), utility 21 (18%). The evidence suggests concentrating on sentimental/unclear, but it cannot decisively choose between them yet, and “unclear” reflects missing intent in the story rather than a true segment label.

root_cause_hypothesis.text: At [stage5], many people begin with minimal cues (often single nouns or a named entity); Photos’ search then misparses the entity or lacks the concept/object, returning irrelevant, too-broad, or zero results, or burying the match — so the remembered-but-vague photo never becomes visible for recognition.

intelligence_needed.text: Insert an AI capability at [stage5] that can: interpret and expand single-noun or named-entity cues; recover from entity misparsing; match higher-level concepts when specific objects are unrecognized; manage recall/precision when results are far too many; and elevate likely matches above the fold or propose near-hits to pivot when the exact match is elusive — areas explicitly reflected in the observed failure modes and result patterns, with near-hit pivots rarely seen in public stories (1 of 115).

falsifiers.text: In interviews, people typically start with rich multi-keyword or full natural descriptions rather than single-noun or entity queries, undermining the premise that terse cues drive failure at [stage5].
Participants do not report irrelevant, over-broad, or zero-results pages as common outcomes; instead they feel the results match their cues well.
Memory gaps (not search matching) emerge as the primary first failure, with many more stories stalling at [stage2] than suggested by public stories (currently 6 of 115).

People routinely succeed by using a near-hit to anchor and pivot; if this becomes common in interviews, the need for AI to bridge vague-to-target within search results weakens (public stories show 1 of 115).

caveats.text: Thin evidence base: 115 core stories, below the 300 the engine was designed for; only one candidate clears the evidence floor — [stage5] passes both gates and is ranked, while others are below floor or gated out.

Coding reliability is “ok” (kappa 0.60) but not correctness; several fields are low-reliability and barred from headlines and scores (e.g., metric_node, outcome, q:2.1), so any signals from those should be treated as exploratory only.
Public talk about not finding a photo is mostly about photos that are gone (adjacent 130 of 216 at [stage0]), which can skew perception away from vague-but-present retrieval problems.
Large gaps remain in the codebook: 28 of 60 questions go to interviews (including several 5.x items about result quality and matching), so we should expect new detail that could shift the hypothesis.

content.label: A hypothesis to be validated in the Part 3 interviews — not a finding.

facts.text: 31235 public records were read; 331 are retrieval stories from 316 people; 115 are core (a known photo, vaguely remembered) from 109 people, and 216 adjacent. The engine was designed for at least 300 core stories; every share is of coded public stories, never a retrieval success rate, a share of users or a share of searches.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 9 (outcome — nothing went wrong): 38 of 115 (33%), from 33 people. By photo type: sentimental 17, unclear 15, utility 6.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 5 (search did not understand or match the cue): 31 of 115 (27%), from 30 people. By photo type: unclear 15, sentimental 13, utility 3.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 0 (library state (the photo was never there or was gone)): 20 of 115 (17%), from 20 people. By photo type: utility 8, sentimental 6, unclear 6.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 3 (strategy — where and how they looked): 9 of 115 (8%), from 9 people. By photo type: sentimental 6, unclear 3.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 6 (recognition — hard to spot in the results): 9 of 115 (8%), from 9 people. By photo type: unclear 6, sentimental 3.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 2 (memory — could not remember enough): 6 of 115 (5%), from 6 people. By photo type: utility 4, sentimental 1, unclear 1.
Core stories whose FIRST failure is Stage 1 (trigger and intent): 2 of 115 (2%), from 2 people. By photo type: sentimental 2.
Core stories by photo type: sentimental 48 of 115 (42%), unclear 46 of 115 (40%), utility 21 of 115 (18%). 'unclear' means the story does not say why the photo was kept.

Among adjacent stories, 130 of 216 (60%) first fail at Stage 0: the photo was deleted, never backed up or elsewhere. Most public talk about not finding a photo is about photos that are gone, not vaguely remembered.
Question 5.6 (what search showed them), core stories that answered it, of 115 asked: irrelevant_results 6, far_too_many 3, zero_results 2.
Question 3.2 (how they looked inside Google Photos), core stories that answered it, of 115 asked: search_bar_keywords 23, timeline_scroll 14, combined_search_then_scroll 3, ask_photos 1.
Question 4.1 (first query shape), core stories that answered it, of 115 asked: single_noun 19, several_keywords 4, full_natural_description 1, named_entity 1.
Core stories that remember WHAT was in the photo: 47 of 115 (41%). [rests on 2.1, low_reliability]
Core stories that remember WHEN it was taken: 24 of 115 (21%). [rests on 2.1, low_reliability]
Core stories that say they forgot the date or year: 13 of 115 (11%).
Core stories that reveal a cue they were certain of and later found WRONG (2.2): 0 of 115 (0%).
Core stories that say the results reminded them of something new (6.5): 1 of 115 (1%).
Core stories that used a near-hit to reach the target (anchor and pivot): 1 of 115 (1%).
Core stories that used a workaround outside search: 9 of 115 (8%).

A second model re-coded 100 stories: primary stage agreement 69%, kappa 0.60 (ok). Low-reliability fields, barred from headlines and scores: metric_node, outcome, q:1.1, q:1.3, q:1.5, q:1.6, q:2.1, q:2.3, q:2.6, q:3.1, q:6.1, q:7.1, q:7.5, q:8.1, severity. Agreement is consistency, not correctness.

28 of 60 codebook questions are answered by too few public stories (over 85% not stated) and go to the interviews: 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 1.4, 2.5, 2.8, 3.3, 3.4, 4.3, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 6.6, 6.7, 8.3, 8.4, 9.2, 9.3, 9.5, 9.6, 10.1, 10.2.

Emerging themes found after the codebook (counts only, not ranked): Search refuses a word as sensitive 5; A Spotlight, collage or Memory can't be found again 3; Can't search within one album 2; Looked in another photo app or service 8.
